en: *Supplement to the Compendium of the True Source*,
compiled by the Tiantai lineage-holding śramaṇa Guoqing Dazhen.
The Dharma heirs of Chan Master Nao of Xingshan (two disciples of Xueqiao Xin):
Master Yongqing Yuanfeng Qing of Wulin ascended the hall and said: "Xuefeng rolling the ball, Daowu dancing with his staff—playing for cleverness only to create clumsiness.
Bimoye’s trident, Jiangmo’s sword—each brought about their own defeat. Xuansha’s tiger, Zihu’s dog."
Be careful not to speak of it; if you speak of it, horns will grow upon your head.
Master Xiu Chan of Tongwen at Xiangfu Monastery in Quzhou ascended the hall and said: "When the occasion arises, he points directly to the face;

when facing the occasion, one must act with swiftness. If you do not know how to turn yourself around, you will waste a thousand-jin effort. Small Assembly: As the late Master De once said, "To perfume..."

The wind comes from the south; a faint coolness arises at the corner of the hall. The Master said, "At Xiangfu, it is not so: 'A gust after gust of north wind, the fragrance of plum blossoms strikes the nose.
If you are like one who waits by a stump for a rabbit, you will surely end up leaning against a wall or propped up by a pillar.
He took up his staff and drove them all back together.
Master Huàn Bái Kě, a Dharma successor of Master Mínxiū Yì, ascended the hall at Luóhàn Monastery in Sīchuān and said: "Eighteen, nineteen—the mouth is born behind the elbow;
Jiáoliáo’s tongue is a scene of total exposure. When I, this mountain monk, speak thus, it is much like begging on the street corners of the marketplace."
"Child, take one coin and buy a sesame cake. Then, before the precious imperial banquet, thump your chest and ribs and say:
'How many people can truly know such a flavor? Should those who understand hear this, it would not merely cause them to spit out their food.
Thus, now, pines are straight and brambles are crooked; cranes are white and crows are black; the wind whistles through the branches and the rain breaks the clods of earth at Mount Dongye."
High! The Qinchi water is cold; each and every thing reveals the constant light. It does not depend on cultivation or fabrication.
Those with eyes see it; those with ears hear it. (He raises his staff upright. Stop, stop! Though you may speak well of the principles, take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.

Chan Master Yian Yin of Xingshan, a successor of Chan Master Poshan Ming of Guanzhong, was a native of the Liao family from Chengdu in Western Sichuan. On the occasion of the Buddha’s Birthday, he ascended the hall and said:
"The past is already past; the future is beyond reckoning. Year after year on the eighth day of the fourth month, everyone celebrates."

The Buddha’s birthday is uniquely honored on this day alone; yet today, its calamities and harms pervade everywhere. Had it not fallen into the functional pivot of Yunmen, how could there be such boundless resources for our veneration?
Since the assembly has together looked up in reverence, do you still see the Old Śākyamuni? [He] raises his whisk and says:
"Not involving past, present, or future, the entire body of reality is fully manifested upon the tip of a hair."
Chan Master Baizhang Mintu of Sichuan ascended the hall and said: "Once you recognize the One, all matters are finished.
Zhaozhou hangs a gourd on the eastern wall; Daowu dances with his ritual tablet without ceasing.
You worthy ones, if there are no idle affairs in your hearts, this is truly a fine season for humanity."
The Dharma Heirs of Chan Master Feiyin Rong (three persons):
Chan Master Dongming Guyun Xingjian of Qiantang, Hangzhou; son of the Song family of Jiaxing. Ascending the hall, he said:
The twenty-fifth day of the tenth month. One must strictly avoid being careless or superficial. A single phrase, free from self-interest, is like the sun at its zenith.
Turning over directly beneath it, one transcends Buddhas and patriarchs. How laughable are Xuefeng rolling the ball and Heshan beating the drum! The functioning of a great man surpasses all others;
how could he ever be content to stake a pole and row a boat? Small Precept Lifting Ceremony *Xichan*: On this spring morning of lifting the retreat, it is best to set out on a pilgrimage.
Neither in the mundane nor the supramundane should one cling; with lively grace, wander beyond the realm of things. Do not, by any means, bind yourself where there are no ropes.
The practice of the patch-robed monk is extraordinary; Buddhas and Patriarchs have always been difficult to grasp. Liberated from all dependence, one attains freedom;
walking alone in the Great Square, heaven and earth are vast and open. The Master passed away in the *Xinchou* year of the Shunzhi era. A stupa was built to the east.

Ming. On the occasion of the conclusion of the retreat, Chan Master Taibai of Yuyang in Mingzhou ascended the hall and said: "Before the fifteenth day, the pond is opened but does not wait for the moon;
after the fifteenth day, the pond is complete and the moon comes of its own accord. Right on the fifteenth day—" [he held up] a fishing pole.
The staff follows him wherever he goes; he performs his play as the occasion arises. At every place, green willows are fit for tethering horses; in every house, there is a road leading to Chang’an.
Chan Master Donglian Gufeng Ruan of Hangzhou, a native of the Xu family of Jiaxing, ascends the hall. The cold clouds part.
The mists at dawn disperse; the warm sun shines upon the empty hall. All things begin from this moment; all is revealed without concealment.

The sprouts of spiritual potential emerge from long-held seeds; the withered roots turn a faint yellow. In the imperial gardens, fragrant flowers have not yet blossomed, yet they vie for their scent, bathed in the auspicious qi.
The exposed clay ox turns its body and leaps forth; ancient relics stir and emit radiance. Truly, the raw jade is revealed.
The golden peaks and ridges raise their brows and dance; the lanterns and pillars bow their heads in praise. To speak exhaustively:
the gate welcomes manifold auspiciousness and boundless splendor. Each and every one joyfully encounters this fine season; naturally, the Way is prosperous and the times are peaceful.
Although it is thus, as for this very same radiant and lovely scenery—after a long silence, he said: "Ultimately, by whose power of grace is it sustained? He then said: "The Original."
The power of harmony turns back heaven and earth; it disperses into forests and peaks, where ten thousand flowers bloom in spring.

[Ascending the hall: To understand speech is not a matter of the tongue; to be able to speak is not a matter of sound. If you can directly attain profound realization, you will no longer traverse the path. The essential meaning is perfectly clear.
[Holding up the staff and shaking it, he said: "The lotus leaf moves without a breeze; there must be fish swimming beneath. [Ascending the hall.]
A man of great character, let not your resolve be extinguished. You must exert fierce effort to emerge from the depths.
Today the Zen barrier is sealed once more; let the white sweat flow for one more time. If you penetrate the source and understand where it falls, the eye of mind will suddenly open.
Holding it crosswise or using it upside down, deploy it as you please; within a single hair-tip, the myriad phenomena of the ocean of lands are contained. Uncreated and beyond all extremes...

Arrangements were made. With a heart full of joy and satisfaction, his smile filled his cheeks. Having perfected the essential matter through a hundred days of practice, he has developed the horns of a great ox to await the spring thunder.
The Master was born in the *wànmǎ* year of the Wànlì era (1615) and passed away on the twenty-eighth day of the eighth month of the *gēngwǔ* year of the Kāngxī era (1710).
His stupa was erected at the foot of Níngyún Peak behind the temple. He was seventy-six years of age and forty-six years of *lǎ* (seniority since ordination).
There exists the *Zhengxùdēng* (Lamp of the Successive Lineage),
which circulates in the world. Chan Master Wànrú Wéi,
a dharma successor of Nánhú Dūmén Pǔjì Jièwéizhōu, whose secular surname was Zhào from the region of Chǔ and Mǐnshuǐ— ascending the hall, he struck the sounding block.
Holding up his staff, he said: "The mind is not the Buddha; wisdom is not the Way.
This staff leaps up to the Thirty-three Heavens, strikes Śakra’s nostrils, and gives a sneeze that falls upon everyone’s eyebrows, where it becomes entangled."
One cannot shake it off by any effort. Even if one were able to shake it off, one would still be three feet in the dark before those with clear eyes.
You must be extremely careful.
(Two disciples of Chan Master Hongjue Mian).
Master Lan of the Benyi lineage composed a verse on the "Old Woman Throwing Her Child": "This child is not even worth sparing;
With tiger-head and horned head, he emerges from the wild fields. As venomous as a scorpion and as fierce as a falcon— Which general could compare to him, even Han Xiaoyao?"
Chan Master Shangcai Rong of Ezhou, a native of the Luo family from Haining in the Central Plains, ascended the hall and said:
"The western wind rustles, hastening the cold trees; Yellow leaves flutter, covering the ground in gold. The crying has already been stilled—who is this weeping softly?"
"Clearly laid bare is the heart of the Patriarch; take it up with urgency, do not be negligent. Suddenly, winter ends and spring arrives again.
The Master passed away in the Dingwei year of the Kangxi era. His verse says: "This year I am sixty-six; in all matters, everything is complete."
Turning over, he hides within the Big Dipper; the mountains are green and the waters are blue. The stupa is located to the right of the Southern Creek.

This is the informal discourse by Chan Master Shizhou Ying of Qingquan, Tongcheng, successor to Chan Master Muchunmen. In various quarters, they practice the seven-day retreat; at Huishan, we practice the three-day retreat.
"Three in the morning, four in the evening; four in the evening, three in the morning. Though the tongs and hammers differ, the color of the fire is surely the same.
As for the *vajra* circle and the *kṣāra-kaṇṭaka* (the bristly chestnut), let you all swallow them or leap over them as you please. Examine this closely upon the forehead of the true host.
[The Master] draws a line with his staff and says: "If you can pass through this furnace and forge, I grant you leave from your meditation session."

If you cannot penetrate this, listen for a moment to this mountain monk’s single pointing-out. *He lets out a shout.* The retreat has ended. The spring mountains are covered in snow; the spring grasses are sprouting.
The spring days are harmonious and mild; the spring breeze blows gently. The patch-robed monks’ straw sandals itch; they long only to wade through waters and climb mountains.
The elder’s staff wavers, having truly succeeded in casting a brick to draw forth a jade gem. Last year’s retreat was concluded.
This too follows the directions and accords with the seasons; this year’s interpretation concludes thus. What harm is there in counting the days early from beginning to end?
The Buddha-dharma is like the moon in the water: long and short, all are perfectly luminous and full. Where there is a Buddha, one must not dwell;
this is the Patriarch’s intent upon the tips of the hundred grasses. Where there is no Buddha, pass by in haste; at every door is the road to Chang’an. Three thousand li.
Externally, you must not err in your conduct. The wall has ears; the walls have ears. If that is so, then you will not go. Why do you strike me again for no reason?
"Picking the willow flowers, picking the willow flowers"—to deliberate and hesitate is to be separated by a thousand differences.
At such a time, tell me: are Tiantai and Yandang Mountains places one may visit or not? Are Mount Touzi and Mount Fushan places one may reach or not?
[He] arrived. After a long silence, he said: "Do not let your idle learning and intellectual understanding bury the mind of the Patriarch.
Chan Master Lingtang Lin of Xianghu Lake in Xiaoshan was a dharma heir of Chan Master Shiqiyun. He was the son of the Shen family of Huating and entered the dharma under Yiyu of Huashan.
The Master underwent tonsure and traveled extensively to study under various masters. He subsequently visited Xuedou, where he received the transmission of the Dharma.

Upon ascending the hall for a formal discourse, he said: "Last night the west wind brushed against the Stone Dragon; this morning we meet face-to-face once again. The message within this is fundamentally no different;
it is but an image of the old Lord Vairocana. In the Wushen year of the Kangxi era, the Master passed away, leaving behind this verse: "Coming, not a single thread; departing, not a..."
A single line. Seventy-two years. A flash of lightning in the void. Casting off all constraints, he sings aloud and returns home.
As he departs, he brandishes the "Blow-off-All-Hair" sword. He lets out a roar and passes away in an instant.
The National Teacher Min, the attendant Wanyin Shengyi of Jinhua Zhiyan, repeatedly urged him to appear in the world [to teach], but the Master was unwilling.
He once posed five questions, the first of which was: "Why does a person who has already responded to 'One' not turn their head back when called?
Second: "From the beginning there has been no front or back; everyone has a nostril. Why then can it not be grasped? Third: "It is precisely because it is too near."
4. Why does one whose capacity is like a flash of lightning refuse to nod at the Dragon-Taming Pagoda?
5. Carrying the bamboo staff wherever you go, performing the play as the occasion demands; why then is it said that the staff is no longer in your hand? 6. Two waters merge into one flow.
For what reason did he arrive before the Thousand-Fathom Cliff? Thereupon, [his body] was torn asunder into seven pieces and eight fragments.
The Dharma Heir of Chan Master Fushí Xián (two individuals):
Chan Master Míhè Lǐ of Fǎhuá at Fēngjiāng, Sūzhōu, ascends the hall. "The Dharmakāya is formless; the cherry..."
Fruit ripens upon the spring branches; the Dharma-eye is without flaw. The fisherman sings his song upon the raft at the river’s edge;

leaning on his staff, he gazes idly into the distance. Ten thousand *li* of mountains and rivers—a fine way of life. Ascending the hall, [he said]: "The meaning of the Patriarchs and the *tathāgata-dhyāna*:

the monkey cries out in the Ba Gorges; the waters stretch wide across the Xiang River. If you do not understand, listen as the moon sets behind the mountain pass and the rooster crows to mark the passing of the night. If..."
A flash of insight! Like clouds parting over Mount Hua, one stands on horseback and gazes.
Chan Master Mei Qiao of Baoning in Jinling ascended the hall and, raising his whisk, said: "When deluded, one is deluded by this very thing.
Holding the 'Night-Bright Talisman' in hand, how many know when day breaks? He struck the whisk and said: "Awakening is awakening to this very thing."
"This very thing—smashing the peach pit, do you still see the old kernel?

He sets down the whisk and says, "Even if you were to exhaust all minds of delusion and enlightenment, it would be like applying moxibustion to a healed scar. Is there anyone who can utter a single phrase that transcends all categories?
He tosses away the whisk and says, "Save your eyebrows."
The Dharma heirs of Chan Master Linye Qi (two persons):
Chan Master Fengxue Yune Xi of Ruzhou was the son of the Chen family of Ziyang in Shu. He traveled extensively to study under various masters throughout the land.
In the evening, he entered Tiantong to attend upon Master Linye Qi. One day, while attending to Qi as they walked in the mountains, his mind was suddenly cleared and his doubts completely dissolved.
He immediately presented a verse, saying: "Enough, enough! Rest, rest! Lying across and sleeping supine upon the mountain mounds, I turn over and crush the very bones of empty space;
The myriad phenomena and the vast cosmos smile and nod their heads. Master Qi nodded in approval. Later, he opened the Dharma.
Pujie. Next, he moved to Longchi and Fengxue. Small Assembly: To take the mind and make it into a Buddha is to gouge out one’s own flesh to patch a wound;
to realize delusion and return to the truth is to pour oil onto a fire. To carry the burden before the pivot of the mechanism is to find a thousand differences on level ground;

to directly accept it is for white clouds to stretch ten thousand miles. If you do not act in this way at all, you will enter the Avīci Hell. When walking, simply walk; when sitting, simply sit; when hunger comes, eat.
Eating a meal; when drowsy, one goes to sleep. This merely results in a single flavor of the ordinary, yet it is still not the matter of the Zen monk’s upward path.
Why? "The three-faced cat treads upon the moon; the two-headed white ox holds smoke in its hands."
Chan Master Jingshou Daoan of Mount Jing, a native of the Zheng clan from Shanyin in the capital of Kyoto, addressed the assembly:

"A blink of an eye or a raising of an eyebrow has already missed the mark; brandishing a mallet or holding up a whisk falls into the second or third [level of conceptualization]. Reaching this point, one must let go of everything with the whole body."
To know directly where one returns is to have a slight measure of comparison. If you engage in calculation or lingering reflection, you are truly like a dull pigeon caught in a whirlwind;
you should merely remain perched within the fence, for how could you soar beyond the clouds? *Small Assembly:* "Once you recognize the One, all things are finished.
Set aside the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; put the studies of precepts, concentration, and wisdom out of mind. Horse...
Master San’s three jars of sauce; Touzi’s one bottle of oil. The flavors are frequently added to the mouth.
Chan Master Langshan Yu of Puming Temple in Jiaxing, successor to Chan Master Shiban Xi, ascended the hall and said: "The fragrant breeze is cool; summer days are long. White clouds..."
Vast and serene. The flowing waters are azure; yellow orioles sing among the green trees. The morning sun shines upon the empty hall. The final word is beyond concealment.
People dwell in a world of fragrant lotus blossoms. Its elegance and clarity are fully manifest. Small Assembly (Xiao Can): Clouds rise and bring rain;
dew solidifies into frost. All is distinct and clear; throughout the entire realm, nothing is hidden. [The Master] brandishes his whisk and says: "Mysterious."
Shaxuan was originally Xie Sanlang.
Zen Master Jianqian of Danyuan in Jizhou, a successor of Chan Master Wuchai, ascended the hall and said: "Face-to-face, it is clear and manifest, yet people do not recognize it. One—
A single sphere, luminous and bright; neither form nor non-form. Its name cannot be grasped, its shape cannot be defined. Two eyebrows cover the bridge of the nose;
there is nothing to know and nothing to understand. Linji, that little fellow, is a white-handed thief. It is not mind, it is not Buddha.
Before the gate lies a pool of water, reflecting through to the very bones of empty space.

Chan Master Nanyue Dashi Tianpei Jian, successor to Chan Master Shanxizhe, addressed the assembly: "Today, Great Goodness (Dashi) begins the formal retreat. I exhort you, brothers, each to be meticulous.
Throughout the two six-hour periods of the day and night, do not let your attention be divided. Single-mindedly observe your own nostrils."

Not only must dullness and distraction be completely swept away, but all that was previously realized must also be discarded. There is no need to laboriously inquire further about the Zen of the Patriarchs;
there is no need to laboriously inquire again about the Primary Meaning. Śākyamuni Buddha was not impressive; Bodhidharma the Patriarch was merely acting out of character.
Though the three thousand and seven hundred [cases] are transcendent and extraordinary, when this mountain monk examines them, they are all not it. Since they are transcendent and extraordinary...
"What is not so? After a long silence, he let out a sigh and said, "Investigate!
This is the small assembly instruction of Chan Master Tan Zhao Ming of Dabeisi, Jiangyin, Changzhou, successor to Chan Master Jieyan Xiu. There is a phrase that is taken for granted.
Do not show it lightly. Riding a bull up Mount Kunlun, he tramples out the marrow of empty space. A tiny gnat’s eyes turn red with urgency; within the realm of Vairocana, dust and smoke arise.
Before the hall, the pillar has long been pregnant; the child born therein is full of spirit. After a long silence, he said:
"What words are these? *Small Assembly* (Xiao Can): Everywhere they present themselves, yet they greedily sleep through the dawn; Mañjuśrī loses the morning light. Eyes...
He even struck out his own eyes. He laughs to death Zi, Chou, Yin, and Mao. How many Meng Bala-erhs are there? Their entire bodies have entered the wild weeds.
Look directly at the mountain colors and the sound of the stream; on the coral branches, the sun shines bright and clear. Small Assembly: Old Man Deshan took up a single staff;
whether it was a Buddha who came or a Mara who came, he struck them both. His eyes were empty of the four seas, and he carried [the world] upon his back.

Sumeru! Mastery over giving and taking, killing and bringing to life—these manifest before you. Yet, if you arrive at the gate of a true monk, you will not even have a share in sweeping the floor or removing excrement.
You lot, you yellow gourds and eggplants—when have you ever recognized what is good or evil?

Chan Master Poyupok of Wanshan on Mount Lu was a dharma successor of Chan Master Jide Li. He was the son of the Zhu family of Gulião. In his youth, he relied upon Fuhu Temple in Luzhou to receive the tonsure.
He went forth to visit Cheryuan of Ruiguang Temple to receive full ordination and took up the koan of the "Bamboo Ruler. Later, he sought instruction from Sanfeng You.
In his later years, he attained a thorough penetration of the Linji school’s essential tenets under [Master] Bang. Subsequently, he met Lingyin Li, with whom his spiritual faculties were in accord;

Lingyin appointed him as the Second Seat. He later went forth to reside at Jiaoshan in Jingkou and subsequently established Wanshan. Entering the hall, he held his staff horizontally across his chest and said:
At Mount Ling, they spoke of the moon; from error, error was transmitted. At Caoxi, they pointed to the moon; taking what was mistaken as correct.
The old monks of the world paid a high price for vermilion, following the heterodox and pursuing the evil. Now, with a single blow from the new Haimen, all under heaven has fallen into darkness.

To cause the sages of antiquity and the worthies of later generations to emerge far beyond the confines of the obvious, if this is not yet so, I shall shift the clouds and meet you all in another way.
He then threw down his staff and descended from the seat. A monk asked, "What is the Buddha?
The Master said, "Alas, you fellow Meng! The monk bowed. The Master said, "Using diligence to compensate for clumsiness."
Chan Master Jiaying Puming Ziyuan, successor to Chan Master Langshan Yu, ascended the hall. A monk asked, "What is the past mind?"
The Master said, "Zhaozhou’s robe weighs seven catties. [The student] asked, "What is the future mind?
The Master said, "Riding a cow while already on a cow—this would make people laugh to death. [The student] asked, "What is the future mind?
The Master said, "There is no need to hang a red lantern beneath the sun. [The student] asked, "Among the three minds, which one attains Buddhahood? The Master said, "Adding further to the blue sky."
A bitter grievance! He then said: "There is no dharma before one's eyes; the meaning lies right before one's eyes. When hungry, eat; when weary, sleep. Striking the meditation seat, he said:
"The fish of the Three Rivers leap through the net; the Kunlun rides the elephant while the egret leads the way. On the occasion of his birthday, he gave a small *can* (sermon), saying:
"Upāṭya, you must remember that at the moment of emerging from the mother’s womb, there was a public case (*kōan*) that has never yet been raised."

Today we cannot avoid this; such an opportunity is difficult to encounter again. I offer this to my brothers. After a long silence, he said: "The Yellow River clears itself only once every three thousand years.
When Puming retired from his abbacy, he ascended the hall and said: "The dwelling place of a man of the Way originally has no fixed direction.

When moving, it is like drifting clouds; when still, it is like the valley spirit (*guǐshén*). Clouds follow the dragon; wind follows the tiger. Taking charge wherever one is, meeting conditions as they arise, that is the source."
At times, he hides his name and conceals his traces atop solitary peaks; at other times, he debates right and wrong at the crossroads.
As a guest, he remains a guest from beginning to end; as a host, he remains a host from beginning to end. Entirely without dependence, he is free and at ease wherever he may be.
Do you know where this mountain monk finds his joy? Having said this, he struck out with his staff.
Master Weiyang Jinghui, a Dharma successor of Master Xianyu Chan, delivered a small-scale sermon at Mingde Chan Monastery: "The state of being wide awake does not reside within clarity;
how could a dozing fellow remain in the midst of stupor? Apart from these two paths, where, then, shall one find a place to settle the body and establish one’s life?"
If one says that sleep and wakefulness are non-dual, there is still no fundamental basis upon which to rely. Brothers, do you understand? In the deep forest, the yellow birds seek their companions;

by the green waters, the gulls float beside their mothers as they sleep. At this small *can* (sermon) marking the end of the retreat period, I hold fast at the vital ford, allowing neither ordinary person nor sage to pass.
Yet, if I loosen the single thread, I allow you all to move freely in every direction. Brothers, would it be better to hold fast, or not?
Let it pass; who can recommend this plum fragrance that permeates the very marrow? It follows the spring wind once more toward the lotus pond.

This was the small assembly (xiaochan) given by Chan Master Zichang Ying of Ba’en Temple in Huzhou, a dharma successor of Chan Master Gurong. "Neither mind nor Buddha"—a perfect circle with a dot placed upon it.

"Mind is Buddha. These are like yellow leaves used to stop a child's crying. Yangqi’s donkey, Zihu’s dog, the four provisions, the three mysteries, the donkey’s feet, and the Buddha’s hand—all you fellows of this ilk would find no use for if you entered the gate of Ba’en Monastery; there, sweeping the floors and picking up excrement, none of those things would apply.
Looking at the assembly, he said: "Is there any patriarch here?
This was the informal sermon by Chan Master Tóngchéng Gúlín Dàyí, successor to Chan Master Shízhōu Yíng. "The spring breeze is warm and gentle; the days grow long and the nights short. Green...
The mountains remain as green as ever; heaven and earth continue to revolve as before. Upon the staff of this mountain monk, what has ever been exempt from past and present?
I respectfully address those who seek the profound mystery: the Way is not far, yet people distance themselves from it of their own accord.

On the occasion of the Imperial Birthday, Chan Master Nan-yuan Xin of Xifang in Yangzhou, a dharma successor of Chan Master Yunfeng Shou, ascended the hall and said: "The four classes of people abide in their vocations;

the hundred officials fulfill their respective duties. Together they beat the *rang* blocks to celebrate the Great Peace, drumming upon their bellies to sing of the King’s transformation. Such is their cultivation."
A time of great peace and prosperity—none surpasses this present age. We, the śramaṇas and sons of the Śākya, cultivate the mind through wisdom and discipline the body through precepts.

Entering the monastic community, our tracks are like floating duckweed upon the lakes and seas; we pursue the life of wandering monks, finding refuge among the clouds and waters, dwelling amidst the mists and pines.

Sharing the same teacher and the Dharma, sharing the same sustenance, how shall we repay the kindness of the King and the kindness of the Buddha? Raising his *śakti* (jewel-topped staff), he said: "If you seek it along the way..."
It is as if one were still competing for a fortnight’s journey. In the small assembly (xiaocan), moving forward is insufficient; retreating is still ample.

One knows only the taste of salt, yet how can one know the acidity of vinegar? When the night is deep and the candle has faded, there is nothing else to do but once again take up idle books to read by the moonlight.

Addressing the assembly, he cited Master Xiu of Qingshan, who said: "The spiritual eyes of the masters in various quarters are lofty, and their merit and virtue are great. Within the monastic communities..."
"Everything is orderly. The food and drink are clean. One might say this is difficult to see but easy to approach. Here in my old monk’s place, worldly ties are shallow;
I clear the weeds and break the wild land, and the tea and rice are coarse and simple. One might say this is easy to see but difficult to approach. The Master said:
In the past there was Qingshan; today there is Fengsheng. The same pit has no different soil. But as for this phrase that is neither difficult nor easy—how would you handle it?
A snap of the fingers instantly transcends the thousand sages; a raising of the eyebrows is not the mechanism before one's eyes.
